title: Consolidation case: repair one orders batch without publishing the mistake
goal: Use recovery state, least privilege, tolerant parsing, deduplication, scan evidence, and a publish gate as one incident response.
concept:
Symptom first: the orders dashboard shows five item rows, but the source manifest says the batch should contain three. Ingest is green and consumer lag is zero. Those signals prove movement, not correctness.

Treat the raw batch like a sealed evidence bag: stop publish, preserve the original input and checkpoint, repair into a new candidate, validate the counts, then promote it. Do not edit the visible gold table while still discovering the failure.
example: Batch B22 contains four envelopes: valid o-41 with two items, a duplicate o-41, valid o-42 with one item, and malformed o-43. Naive flattening emits five rows. The repaired result is two orders and three item rows; one duplicate is excluded and one malformed envelope is quarantined.

use_case.when: Use this recovery sequence when a batch passed transport checks but violates a business invariant after parsing, deduplication, or flattening.
use_case.example: A retail order batch is present and on time, yet repeated events and bad JSON inflate the gold item count.
use_case.decision: Contain first when visible data may be wrong. Replay from preserved raw data into an isolated candidate; publish only after explicit reconciliation. For a harmless late batch, normal retry may be enough.

practice: Move the incident through containment, parse, deduplicate, reconcile, and publish. Watch the visible row count stay unchanged until the final gate.
boundary: The browser is a local JavaScript state machine over four synthetic envelopes. It does not run Databricks, Snowflake, Spark, warehouses, permissions, checkpoints, or production SQL.

Block publish and preserve raw evidence

product_sections.title: Databricks: isolate, repair, validate, then let the job DAG publish
product_sections.html:
Use case. Replay preserved bronze records into a candidate table without changing the current gold table.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production workspace, Unity Catalog objects, and a job identity limited to read bronze, write the repair schema, and publish the approved target. Compute can incur cost.

The SQL below is unexecuted vendor code. Exact VARIANT availability and syntax depend on your supported Databricks Runtime.

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW parsed AS
SELECT *, try_parse_json(payload) AS v FROM bronze.orders_b22;CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW deduped AS
SELECT * EXCEPT(rn) FROM (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY ingested_at) rn FROM parsed WHERE v IS NOT NULL) WHERE rn=1;CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE repair.b22_items AS
SELECT event_id, item.value FROM deduped, LATERAL variant_explode(v:items) item;-- Job task publish depends_on validate; run_if: ALL_SUCCESS

Failure/fix. Writing gold inside the parse step makes partial repair visible. Write an isolated candidate, have a separate validation task compare counts, and allow publish only after success. A job DAG does not replace table-level transactions or Unity Catalog privileges.
product_sections.markdown:
Authorized non-production workspace; SQL/YAML unexecuted.

```sql

SELECT *, try_parse_json(payload) AS v FROM bronze.orders_b22;
-- deduplicate by event_id, explode items into repair.b22_items
```

product_sections.title: Snowflake: quarantine parse failures, flatten the candidate, gate the task
product_sections.html:
Use case. Build the same evidence chain in a repair schema, then let a downstream task publish only the reconciled candidate.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production database, schema, warehouse, and task-owning role. Warehouse and task execution can incur credits.

The SQL is unexecuted vendor code.

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE parsed AS
SELECT *, TRY_PARSE_JSON(payload) v FROM bronze.orders_b22;CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE deduped AS
SELECT * EXCLUDE rn FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY ingested_at) rn FROM parsed WHERE v IS NOT NULL) QUALIFY rn=1;CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE repair.b22_items AS
SELECT event_id, f.value FROM deduped, LATERAL FLATTEN(INPUT => v:items) f;CREATE TASK publish AFTER validate AS CALL publish_b22();

Failure/fix. PARSE_JSON can abort on malformed input. TRY_PARSE_JSON exposes a NULL that you must quarantine and count; silently dropping it loses reconciliation evidence. Clustering is a separate, evidence-driven performance choice.
product_sections.markdown:
Authorized Snowflake sandbox; SQL unexecuted.

```sql
SELECT *, TRY_PARSE_JSON(payload) AS v FROM bronze.orders_b22;
-- deduplicate with ROW_NUMBER, then LATERAL FLATTEN into repair.b22_items
CREATE TASK publish AFTER validate AS CALL publish_b22();
```

The local replay shows the changing counts; it does not run a warehouse or task graph.

title: The reply happened after the request—even when its wall clock says earlier
goal: Use a hybrid logical clock to preserve causal order without pretending physical clocks are perfectly synchronized.
concept:
Two office clocks disagree. A reply can appear to happen before the request if you sort only by wall time.

A hybrid logical clock stores (physical, logical). It follows the wall clock when possible. When a received event is already ahead, it keeps that physical value and increments the logical counter.
example: Node A sends at wall time 100 with HLC (100,0). Node B’s clock reads 95. After receiving the message, B replies with (100,1). The reply sorts after the request even though B’s wall clock is behind.

use_case.when: Use HLC timestamps when you need a compact, roughly wall-time-ordered label that respects observed message causality across nodes.
use_case.example: Order changes from two regions are tagged so a received update and its reply cannot be reversed by clock skew.
use_case.decision: Use HLC for causality plus approximate time. Use a consensus log for one authoritative total order, and vector clocks when you need to distinguish concurrency precisely.

practice: Change B’s wall clock from 95 to 105 and watch whether the physical component or logical counter advances.
boundary: This two-node model omits clock bounds, persistence across restart, overflow, concurrent events, and database-specific tie breaking. HLC does not create consensus.
js:
function hlcPaint(){const wall=Number(bClock.value),recvP=100,replyP=Math.max(wall,recvP),replyL=replyP===recvP?1:0;bClockValue.textContent=wall;world.innerHTML='

Lexicographic order: (100,0) < ('+replyP+','+replyL+'). Causality is preserved.

';}bClock.oninput=hlcPaint;hlcPaint();
questions: B wall=95 receives (100,0). Its next HLC is?
The received physical value wins and the logical counter advances.
Observed request sorts before its reply
It preserves the happened-before edge without synchronizing clocks.
One authoritative write order must be agreed by replicas

steps.note: Define the timestamp pair.
Record the request and B wall clock.
Advance B physical time to the larger observed value.
Break the physical-time tie with the logical counter.

walkthrough.limit: Executed on local Java 17 over synthetic timestamps. It did not test a distributed datastore or clock-drift bound.

sources: Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases
visual_explanation: The two lifelines keep their disagreeing wall clocks visible while the arrows carry HLC values; the counter, not a fabricated wall-clock jump, orders the reply.
written_questions: Where would HLC state need durable storage across a service restart?
Which of your ordering requirements actually needs consensus instead?

title: The service is green; the business is not recovered yet
goal: Separate technical restoration, business reconciliation, and systemic prevention instead of declaring victory at the first green dashboard.
concept:
A reopened airport is not fully recovered while thousands of passengers still have wrong itineraries. Likewise, healthy servers are only one recovery clock.

Track three outcomes: service restored, business state reconciled, and systemic control closed. Each needs its own owner and evidence.
example: The pipeline turns green at 10:12. At that moment, 12,400 customer records are still wrong. Replay and reconciliation finish at 11:05. The preventive publish gate is deployed and tested two days later. “Resolved at 10:12” erases most of the work and risk.

use_case.when: Use multiple recovery clocks when an incident leaves durable customer, financial, data, or compliance effects after infrastructure recovers.
use_case.example: A corrected ETL job is healthy, but invoices created during the bad window still need identification and repair.
use_case.decision: Close the technical incident when operations stabilize; keep business remediation and prevention as explicit tracked work with exit evidence.

practice: Move the status marker across the three milestones and decide what statement is safe for customers, leaders, and engineers.
boundary: The dates are illustrative. Real severity, disclosure, audit, legal, and customer-communication duties depend on the organization and incident.

'+x[0]+'
'+x[1]+'

').join('')+'

Safe statement: '+(p===0?'service restored; customer correction still in progress':p===1?'customer impact reconciled; prevention remains open':'recovery and preventive control verified')+'.

title: A valid tool call can still return the wrong shape
goal: Validate MCP structured output against the declared output schema before a model reasons over it.
concept:
A vending machine can accept a valid button press and still dispense the wrong product. Validating tool input is only half the boundary.

An MCP tool may declare an outputSchema. The server must return matching structured content; the client should validate it before passing the result to an LLM.
example: get_order promises {order_id, status}. The handler returns {id, state}. Both objects look plausible to a person, but the contract failed. Treat the result as an error, keep the raw evidence for debugging, and do not invite the model to guess field meanings.

use_case.when: Use result validation for tools whose output feeds model decisions, workflow branching, side effects, or audit records.
use_case.example: An order-support agent calls a tool before deciding whether a refund is allowed.
use_case.decision: Reject schema mismatches at the harness boundary. Add semantic checks for valid-but-impossible values; JSON Schema does not prove business truth.

practice: Switch between the promised and drifted result. Observe that the tool invocation succeeds but the harness gate changes.
boundary: The browser checks only two required field names. Production validation must implement the full negotiated JSON Schema dialect, size limits, untrusted text handling, logging controls, and server identity.

title: Round where the optimizer feels the error, not where the state is stored
goal: See why changing the coordinate used for stochastic rounding can reduce update error in 4-bit optimizer-state quantization.
concept:
Suppose a thermostat stores temperature, but your real concern is heating cost. Equal temperature errors do not create equal cost errors. You may want rounding probabilities to reflect the quantity the system actually uses.

A new paper studies 4-bit AdamW state. It proposes rounding in preconditioner space—closer to the optimizer update—rather than only in stored second-moment space.
example:
A toy value v=0.01 lies between stored levels 0 and 0.04. State-space stochastic rounding chooses zero with probability 0.75. With h(v)=1/(sqrt(v)+0.01), matching the expected preconditioner chooses zero with probability about 0.045. The coordinate changes the probability dramatically.

The authors report reduced mean validation-loss gaps versus TorchAO 4-bit AdamW at every evaluated model size from 130M to 2.7B, with the largest reported reduction 70%. This is a research claim, not a production guarantee.

use_case.when: Potentially useful when optimizer state memory limits training scale and 4-bit quantization error materially changes learning.
use_case.example: Pretraining a billion-parameter transformer where AdamW state consumes scarce accelerator memory.
use_case.decision: Reproduce quality, throughput, memory, kernels, and numerical stability on your exact stack before adoption. Use mature 8/32-bit state when reliability matters more than the extra memory saving.

practice: Move v between 0 and 0.04 and compare the zero probability under the two coordinate systems.
boundary: The browser performs one-cell arithmetic. It omits tensor blocks, exponent selection, ZE-EDEN calibration, first moments, kernels, training dynamics, and every benchmark in the paper.

function quantPaint(){const v=Number(vValue.value)/1000,lo=0,hi=.04,eps=.01,pState=(hi-v)/(hi-lo),h=x=>1/(Math.sqrt(x)+eps),pUpdate=(h(v)-h(hi))/(h(lo)-h(hi));vOut.textContent=v.toFixed(3);world.innerHTML='
Stored-state space
P(round to 0) = '+pState.toFixed(3)+'
Preconditioner space
P(round to 0) = '+pUpdate.toFixed(3)+'

Same endpoints and v; different notion of unbiased error.

';}vValue.oninput=quantPaint;quantPaint();

It targets the transformed quantity used in the update
The optimizer feels the nonlinear preconditioner, not raw v directly.

The reported experiments support further reproduction

title: Build once, promote the same digest
goal: Make production run the exact artifact that passed tests instead of rebuilding something merely similar.
concept:
A sealed meal is inspected, labeled, and sent to the dining room. If the kitchen cooks a new meal after inspection, the approval no longer applies.

CI should build an artifact once, compute its digest, test and attest that object, then promote the same digest through environments.
example: Build produces image digest sha256:aaa. Staging tests it. A production job that rebuilds from the same commit pulls a changed transitive dependency and produces sha256:bbb. The commit matches; the bytes do not. Production is now running an untested artifact.

use_case.when: Use immutable promotion for containers, packages, Lambda bundles, infrastructure plans, and other deployable outputs that cross environments.
use_case.example: Build an API image, attest and test its digest, then deploy that digest to staging and production with environment approvals.
use_case.decision: Promote immutable content when environments should differ only in configuration. Rebuild only when the target platform truly requires it, and then test/attest the rebuilt target separately.

practice: Choose promote or rebuild and change the production digest. See whether the staging evidence still applies.
boundary: The browser compares short labels. Real provenance needs trusted builders, registry immutability, attestation verification, permission boundaries, retention, and environment-specific configuration management.

title: One idempotency key, one create effect
goal: Make a retried create request return the original outcome while rejecting key reuse for different intent.
concept:
A coat-check ticket identifies one stored coat. Presenting the same ticket again should return the same coat, not create another claim.

For a create API, the client sends an idempotency key. The server stores the key, a fingerprint of the intended request, and the result as one durable decision.
example: POST /orders with key k-77 and amount $25 creates o-900. A network timeout hides the reply. Retrying the same key and payload returns o-900 without a second order. Reusing k-77 with $40 is rejected because the intent changed.

use_case.when: Use idempotency keys for client-retried operations that create side effects and cannot safely depend on transport success.
use_case.example: Order creation, payment initiation, job submission, or provisioning requests over an unreliable network.
use_case.decision: Let the caller supply a unique intent key and validate a payload fingerprint. Do not use a server-generated key that the client cannot repeat after losing the response.

practice: Send the first request, a same-payload retry, and a changed-payload reuse. Watch stored state and side-effect count.
boundary: The browser stores one key in memory. Production needs atomic persistence, scope/tenant binding, retention, concurrency control, response replay policy, authentication, and rules for failed/in-progress requests.
